summary:
Lunar Outpost: Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer is an interactive, browser-based educational simulator that transforms complex space engineering principles into hands-on learning. 
Players take command of a simulated four-person lunar habitat, managing interconnected systems for oxygen generation, water recycling, food production, radiation shielding, and power distribution.
Unlike traditional space-themed educational games, our simulator demonstrates how every decision affects the entire habitat. Producing more oxygen consumes water and electricity, excessive CO₂ removal can reduce crop productivity, and increasing reactor output creates additional thermal-management challenges.
Three mission scenarios challenge players to maintain operational stability, respond to simulated solar radiation emergencies, and survive an extended lunar night.
Built using JavaScript, HTML5 Canvas, and CSS, the project draws upon NASA's published life-support research and engineering resources.
Our mission is to make systems thinking, resource management, and space engineering accessible, engaging, and understandable for the next generation of explorers.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

Our simulator lets players manage the life support system (ECLSS) of a 400 m³ lunar outpost for 4 astronauts. In real space habitats, all systems are connected, so fixing one problem can create another:

  • Electrolysis (OGS) splits water into breathable O2 and H2, but uses a lot of electricity and drains drinking water.
  • The Sabatier scrubber cleans exhaled CO2 and turns it back into water, but if you clean too much CO2 (below 250 ppm), the greenhouse plants stop growing food.
  • The Hull Water-Wall protects the crew from solar radiation, but if the internal water tank runs dry, life support starts draining water directly from this protective shield.
  • The 12 kWe Kilopower nuclear reactor gives power during the 14-day lunar night, but 30% of its power leaks into the cabin as extra heat that the air conditioner must cool down.

Core Features and Mechanics

1. Interconnected Life Support Systems

Players control oxygen production through water electrolysis, carbon dioxide removal and Sabatier-based water recovery, hydroponic food production, water recycling, and lunar ice extraction.

These processes interact through shared water, atmosphere, and electricity reserves, creating meaningful engineering trade-offs.

2. Energy and Thermal Management

The habitat combines simulated solar power, battery storage, and a controllable nuclear reactor.

Players must balance electricity generation and consumption while accounting for thermal loads, equipment operation, and changing environmental conditions.

3. Radiation Protection

A dual-purpose water-wall system allows players to transfer water between potable reserves and a radiation-shielding structure.

Additional shielding can be constructed using simulated lunar regolith during extravehicular activities (EVAs).

These mechanics demonstrate how engineering resources can serve multiple competing purposes.

4. Predictive Engineering Assistant

An integrated analytical assistant monitors resource consumption and production trends.

Using numerical rates of change, it estimates approaching shortages and critical operating conditions, providing warnings within a 72-hour prediction horizon.

The assistant encourages proactive planning instead of reacting only after a system failure.

5. Interactive Telemetry and Visual Feedback

The interface combines engineering controls, an animated habitat schematic, system status indicators, a power budget, and a mission log.

Players immediately see how their actions affect oxygen availability, cabin conditions, water reserves, energy storage, food production, and crew safety.

Three Mission Scenarios

Mission 1: Equilibrium Training (168 hours)

Maintain stable habitat operations over seven days while responding to a simulated moderate solar radiation event.

Mission 2: X-Class Solar Flare Crisis (96 hours)

Recover from hazardous atmospheric conditions and prepare the habitat's shielding systems for severe simulated solar radiation events.

Mission 3: Lunar Night Survival (336 hours)

Operate through an extended 14-day lunar night scenario without solar power, relying on battery reserves, reactor output, and careful energy management.

Each scenario introduces distinct technical constraints and requires different operational strategies.

NASA Research Integration

The simulator uses published NASA engineering resources to inform its educational model, including the Life Support Baseline Values and Assumptions Document, Environmental Control and Life Support Systems documentation, Kilopower research, and space radiation protection studies.

The model intentionally simplifies some engineering processes and uses defined simulation parameters. Its telemetry represents the simulated habitat rather than live measurements from an actual NASA spacecraft.

Technical Implementation

The application was developed using:

  • JavaScript for simulation logic and state management.
  • HTML5 for application structure and interactive controls.
  • Canvas API for animated 2D visualization.
  • CSS3 for interface design and responsive layouts.
  • GitHub Pages for public deployment.
  • GitHub for source-code hosting and version control.

The simulation runs entirely in the browser without requiring a backend server or external software installation.

HOW IT WORKS

The web app updates the base physics every 15 minutes of game time (dt = 0.25 h) and shows everything on a live 2D screen:

  • Physics Engine (physics.js): Calculates cabin oxygen pressure (kPa), CO2 level (ppm), crew breathing and eating, water recycling, battery charge, and radiation protection during solar storms.
  • 72-Hour Predictive Assistant: Tracks how fast each resource is falling (dX/dt) and warns the player up to 72 hours before oxygen, water, food, or battery power runs out.
  • Three Missions:
  1. Mission 1: Equilibrium Training (168 h / 7 days) — Learn to balance the base and survive a small solar storm.
  2. Mission 2: X-Class Solar Flare Crisis (96 h / 4 days) — Fix low O2 and high CO2 while filling the Water-Wall before a strong 15 mSv/h solar flare hits at hour 8.
  3. Mission 3: 14-Day Lunar Night Survival (336 h / 14 days) — Survive two weeks of total darkness at -170 °C with 0 kW solar power using only the nuclear reactor and battery.

Innovation and Creativity

Our principal innovation is the combination of interconnected life-support simulation, real-time engineering feedback, and predictive resource analysis within a single accessible educational environment.

Rather than presenting isolated scientific facts or predetermined quiz questions, the simulator creates situations in which learners discover engineering principles through experimentation.

For example, solving an oxygen shortage may create a water shortage, while increasing greenhouse production changes electricity demand and atmospheric conditions.

This interconnected structure encourages players to evaluate the consequences of their actions rather than searching for a single correct answer.

Intended Impact

Lunar Outpost is designed for students, young space enthusiasts, STEM educators, and anyone interested in understanding the engineering challenges of human space exploration.

The project aims to:

  • Develop systems thinking and analytical reasoning.
  • Introduce fundamental principles of spacecraft life support.
  • Demonstrate the importance of resource conservation.
  • Encourage experimentation and engineering problem-solving.
  • Increase interest in aerospace engineering and STEM education.

By turning complex system interactions into observable and controllable processes, our project helps learners understand why sustainable human exploration requires careful coordination of technology, resources, and human decisions.
dataRefs: NASA Life Support Baseline Values and Assumptions Document (BVAD, NASA/TP-2015-218570/REV1) — Used as the reference for typical crew metabolic loads (O2, CO2, water, food, body heat), scaled by us to 4 astronauts per hour, and for the general plant growth/food assumptions.

NASA Spaceflight Human-System Standard Volume 2: Human Factors, Habitability, and Environmental Health — Used for safe cabin limits (hypoxia below 16 kPa O2, fire risk above 30 kPa O2, CO2 poisoning above 10,000 ppm, temperature limits, and the 150 mSv radiation limit).

International Space Station (ISS) ECLSS: ICES-2015-155, “ISS ECLS System Overview of Events 2010–2014” — Used for the ECLSS architecture (water electrolysis OGA, Sabatier CO2 reactor, water recovery WPA/UPA) and for the ~98% water recycling level on the ISS. The ratios 0.89 kg O2 and 0.11 kg H2 per liter of water and 0.818 L water per kg CO2 come from our own stoichiometry calculation. The 95% grey water recycling is our game value, slightly below the real 98%.

NASA Kilopower Reactor (KRUSTY) Nuclear Ground Test Results and Lessons Learned (NASA/TM-2018-219941) — Used as the reference for fission surface power in the Kilopower class (1–10 kWe, day and night independent of sunlight). The 12 kWe maximum and the 30% heat leak into the habitat are our game parameters.

“Exploration Lessons from ISS” — Used for the ECLSS architecture (water electrolysis OGA, Sabatier CO2 reactor, water recovery WPA/UPA) and for the ~98% water recycling level on the ISS. The ratios 0.89 kg O2 and 0.11 kg H2 per liter of water and 0.818 L water per kg CO2 come from our own stoichiometry calculation. The 95% grey water recycling is our game value, slightly below the real 98%.

NASA OLTARIS: On-Line Tool for the Assessment of Radiation in Space (NASA/TP-2010-216722) (tool: https://oltaris.nasa.gov) — Used as the reference for the principle that radiation dose decreases with shielding thickness in g/cm² (GCR vs. solar particle events). The simplified formula sigma = regolith + 0.1 * Wall_L and the attenuation lengths (250 and 22 g/cm²) are our own approximation of that principle.
